# Runner-link config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/runner-link/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.RunnerLinkBlock` — this daemon's own side of the fleet link. A singleton kind: at most one `runner_link` block across the vault.

**The clocks** (ADR-106 D12/D13) are how long a dispatch's result wait survives one absence of the host it was placed on, and how often this daemon re-states each declared runner's link state into the seat ledger. Both are hot-reloadable (ADR-122 D1) — a `reconnect_grace` edit is spent by waits that start after the reload while a wait already open keeps the value it began with, and a `host_meter_interval` edit resets the running reporter's ticker in place.

**`default_host_pool`** (ADR-133 D4) is the one attribute here that is not a clock: it names a declared `pool` that replaces the implicit fleet — the local runner plus every enabled declared runner — deployment-wide, for a fleet whose machines are interchangeable. An explicitly named `seat_pools` set wins over it, because a default fills an axis nobody named and never adds members to an axis somebody did; a deployment whose machines are *not* interchangeable names pools per worker instead. It must name a declared pool, and a **host** pool: a default naming a token pool would draw a credential seat and place the work on no machine at all, so both shapes are refused at `tera config apply`, at boot and in `tera validate` with the same sentence. It is vault-authored and hot-reloadable because it carries the same authority a worker's `seat_pools` already carries and admits work only to machines whose `runner` declarations this vault already holds (ADR-133 D7) — it is **not** the tool-dispatch posture, which stays kernel-owned and restart-bound (ADR-122 D2).

**It is consulted at the draw, and an edit here moves placement without a restart.** `pkg/workorder/bootstrap.BuildSeatPolicy` resolves it into `seatgate.Policy.HostAxis`, which fills the host axis of every dispatch that needs a machine and names no host pool of its own. It reaches the *running* gate on reload by a different path from the two clocks beside it — the seat policy is rebuilt and replaced, rather than reconciled with them — so a dispatch resolving after the edit draws on the new pool while one already placed is untouched, and a Work Order sitting at `blocked:waiting-on-capacity` is re-walked on the same edge.

**The daemon's own host can be named in the pool this points at.** `default_host_pool` REPLACES the implicit fleet deployment-wide, so a deployment that declares one has taken this daemon's host out of placement unless the pool names it back: declare `runner "local" { seats = n }` — bounds-only, with no `api_key_hash`, because this host runs in-process and is never dialled — plus an ordinary admission-only `member "local" {}`, and list that member in the pool (ADR-133 D1 as amended 2026-09-17). Under `mode = "remote_only"` that authoring is refused, because a daemon that will not execute must not be placed on.

The kernel `runner_link {}` block this kind replaced is retired (ADR-122 D5): kept there it would be read once at boot and would silently override every later vault edit.

## Example

A minimal `runner-link`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/runner-link/example-runner-link.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

runner_link {}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reconnect_grace` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `host_meter_interval` | string | no | — | — | — | — |
| `default_host_pool` | string | no | — | — | — | The declared pool this deployment places work on when nothing else names one, replacing the implicit fleet (the local runner plus every enabled declared runner) deployment-wide (ADR-133 D4). Unset keeps the implicit fleet. An explicitly named seat_pools set WINS over it: a default fills an axis nobody named and never adds members to an axis somebody did. It must name a declared pool, and a HOST pool — every member of the named pool supplies admission rather than a value — because a default naming a token pool would draw a credential seat and place the work on no machine at all; both shapes are refused at apply, at boot and in tera validate. Vault-authored and hot-reloadable: it carries the same authority a worker's seat_pools carries and admits work only to machines whose runner declarations this vault already holds. It is NOT the tool-dispatch posture, which stays kernel-owned and restart-bound (ADR-122 D2). |
| `rollout` | block | no | — | — | — | How this daemon brings its fleet to its own build and paces what it sends it (ADR-163 D9/D10): whether a rollout starts by itself or waits to be released (mode), which runner goes first (canary) and how long it soaks (canary_soak), how much of a pool may be upgrading at once (max_unavailable), and how many transfers run at once (max_transfers). Every attribute is optional and none is required. Hot-reloadable. |
| `host` | block | no | — | — | — | The fleet's host policy (ADR-164 D2): disk floors, store caps, sweep ages, release retention, the idle-sleep hold, log level, PATH, pre-placement and the cache bound, for every runner this daemon admits over a runner listener — not the daemon's own host, runner "local", which takes no host policy because its runner uses the daemon's own stores, which platform {} bounds. It is sent to each runner over its link, and never over a plaintext one: a runner on a plaintext link keeps what it last applied. A field a runner's own runner "<id>" { host {} } declares wins over this block's, field by field; a field neither declares falls to a value still written in that host's runner.hcl, then to the binary's default. tera runner log-level and tera runner path on the host win over all of them until cleared. No field here can change where a runner dials, whom it trusts or what key it presents. Hot-reloadable. |

## `rollout` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | string | no | `automatic` | — | — | Whether a rollout starts by itself: "automatic" \| "manual". "automatic" (the default; unset means this, and it is the golden path) starts a rollout once the daemon's boot settles on a build differing from any enabled runner's (ADR-163 D1). "manual" arms the rollout and waits for tera runners rollout release for each build — the standing hold for a deployment that applies migrations between the daemon and its fleet by hand. It decides when a rollout starts, not how it proceeds: the canary and its soak apply in both modes. Hot-reloadable. |
| `canary` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Runners preferred as a rollout's first host (ADR-163 D9.1). An enabled runner named here goes first if any is connected; when none is connected, or the list is unset, the connected runner with the fewest attached dispatches goes first, ties broken by id. A name that matches no connected runner is passed over rather than refused, because a runner a class admits has no runner block of its own to match. A blank entry is refused, and so is "local": this daemon's own host follows the daemon and is never rolled. Hot-reloadable. |
| `canary_soak` | string | no | `10m` | — | — | How long the rollout waits after its canary confirms before offering the build to any other host (ADR-163 D9.1). A duration string like "10m". Unset takes ten minutes, ADR-163's ratified default: long enough for a host's probation and its first dispatches on the new build to surface a fault before the rest of the fleet takes it, and revisable on evidence. "0s" proceeds once the canary's casualty settle — thirty seconds from its confirmation, in which no Work Order placed on it may be newly failed or held (ADR-163 D13.3) — has passed; the soak and the settle run together, and the longer decides. A negative or unparseable value is refused. A canary that reverts, or has a casualty, stops the rollout whatever this says. Hot-reloadable. |
| `max_unavailable` | string | no | `25%` | — | — | How much of any one pool may be upgrading at once, from its offer to its confirmation or revert, as a whole-number percentage of the pool's members such as "25%" (ADR-163 D9.2). The count is the share rounded down and never less than one, so a pool of three takes one host at a time at the default and a pool of eight takes two. A host in several pools is held to the tightest; a runner in no declared pool counts against the implicit fleet as one pool. Unset takes 25%, ADR-163's ratified default: a pool keeps three quarters of its seats while it rolls, and revisable on evidence. It must be above 0% and at most 100%. Hot-reloadable. |
| `max_transfers` | integer | no | `4` | — | — | How many transfers this daemon runs at once across its fleet. It is the one bound pre-placement and the rollout share (ADR-163 D10, ADR-164 D9): a host's pre-placed vault directories and its toolchain provisioning each hold one while they run, and a rollout's transfer of a release to a host holds one from its offer until the host answers that it staged it or could not. Unset takes 4; it must be at least 1. A transfer past the bound waits for one to finish — a rollout's next host is offered once a slot is free — and a dispatch never does: one that needs what is mid-placement joins that transfer. A reload applies a changed bound to the transfers started after it. |

## `host` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `min_free_disk` | string | no | `20GB` | — | — | The hard free-space floor for the filesystem holding the runner's data_dir: below it the host reports its disk meter exhausted and the daemon stops sending it work (ADR-106 D13). A size in the daemon's byte-size grammar, powers of 1024: 20GB, 500MB, 1.5TB, 20Gi, 500MiB, or a bare byte count. Unset takes 20GB; "0" is how an operator says they want no floor at all, which is why the default is applied to an absent value rather than to a zero. It is a flat reserve, not a prediction: nothing estimates what the next dispatch will need, because the host that would have to make that estimate does not know what the next dispatch is. |
| `warn_free_disk` | string | no | — | — | — | The optional soft floor, which must be ABOVE min_free_disk as the two resolve for the host; between the two the host reports warning. A floor pair whose warning band is empty is refused, naming where the hard floor came from. Read this before setting it: ADR-092 D9 ranks the status band ahead of any reading, so warning is a hard deprioritization and not a nudge — a warned host with 40 GB free loses to one at 99% full that is still ok. It means "prefer any other host in this pool"; where that is not the intent leave it unset, since the fullness reading is already on tera runners list as telemetry. Same size grammar as min_free_disk. |
| `git_mirror_store_cap` | string | no | `2GB` | — | — | The host's ceiling on the total size of its ADR-128 local git object mirror store — the donor a git workspace binding borrows objects from, so a dispatch transfers the commits since the last fetch rather than the repository. Each host holds its own store, under <data_dir>/volumes/persistent/git-object-mirror/, because the clone is performed by the machine that provisions the workspace. Same size grammar as min_free_disk. Unset is the same finite 2GB ADR-128 D8 ratified for the daemon; there is no spelling for unbounded, and "0" is refused rather than read as one. It bounds the host's store and not the daemon's, which is platform { git_mirror_store_cap }. |
| `tracked_checkout_store_cap` | string | no | `2GB` | — | — | The host's ceiling on its one store of commit trees (ADR-150 D1, ADR-168 D1): the immutable per-commit trees a mount on the host holds, and the object store they are read out of, together. It bounds a Work Order reference's trees as well as a tracked checkout's: both are held in the one store. Each host holds its own store, under <data_dir>/tracked-checkouts/, and materializes every tree a mount there holds from its own fetch; it never borrows the daemon host's trees. Unheld trees are collected first, least recently used; a mount that would still exceed the ceiling while every tree is held is refused, saying so, and a held tree is never evicted. Same size grammar and fail-closed rules as git_mirror_store_cap: unset is a finite 2GB, and "0" or a malformed size is refused. |
| `max_failed_dispatch_age` | string | no | `336h` | — | — | How long the host keeps the directory of a FAILED dispatch that no daemon is ever going to answer for (ADR-137 D9). It is not a second retention rule: the daemon's reclaim frame decides whether a failed dispatch's directory is kept, and this bounds only the case where that decision never arrives — a decommissioned runner, or one moved to a daemon that knows nothing of its history. It is applied by the start sweep, and again whenever its value changes, and only to a terminal directory — its control socket dead, and its result on disk or its death already reported — so a live dispatch is never touched however long it has run. A Go duration string: 336h, 72h, 30m; there is no d unit. Unset takes fourteen days, a starting point revisable on evidence rather than a measurement; "0" means no ceiling at all, for a host kept for forensics. A negative duration is refused. |
| `keep_releases` | integer | no | `1` | — | — | How many releases installed BEFORE current the host keeps for tera runner rollback (ADR-137 D7, the release sweep's rule 3). It is rollback depth and nothing else: the release the running supervisor started from, the one current names, and every release a dispatch record names are kept whatever this says, so no value here removes a release something is executing from. While a rolled upgrade is on probation, the release its probation record names as the one the host ran before is kept too, whatever this says and 0 included, because that is where probation's revert moves to (ADR-163 D7); a probation record that cannot be read keeps every release. That is why 0 is admissible — it means no rollback depth, and rollback then refuses by name. A whole number, not a string: a count has no unit. Unset takes 1, which is exactly what one rollback moves to. A negative count is refused. |
| `prevent_idle_sleep` | boolean | no | `true` | — | — | Whether the host asks not to idle-sleep while it is executing a dispatch (ADR-106 D12 amendment A5). Unset means it does; false is the opt-out. It exists because idle sleep during a dispatch is not something an operator chose: a Mac on battery slept with a dispatch running, its link dropped, and the Work Order was held at blocked:runner-unreachable for 39 minutes against a session that had finished its work. On darwin it is a PreventUserIdleSystemSleep assertion and nothing stronger — a closed lid and a deliberate sleep still sleep the machine; platforms with no mechanism wired take nothing. Reach for false where the machine must be free to sleep on its own schedule and a dropped dispatch is acceptable, such as a laptop that is a fleet host incidentally. |
| `log_level` | string | no | `info` | — | — | The level the runner logs at: debug, info, warn or error. A person on the host can override it with tera runner log-level, --log-level or $TERA_RUNNER_LOG_LEVEL, and an override wins over every level declared here until it is cleared with tera runner log-level default (ADR-164 D4). Any other value is refused. |
| `path` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Directories the runner puts ahead of the PATH its service states, in order — where it looks up the toolchains and handlers a dispatch execs. Each entry is an absolute directory and holds neither the PATH list separator nor a line break; anything else is refused, and so is a list that names no directory. Unset leaves the service's PATH as it is. A person on the host can override it with tera runner path, which wins until cleared with tera runner path default (ADR-164 D4). A runner takes a changed path at its next start. |
| `preplace` | boolean | no | `true` | — | — | Whether the daemon pre-places what this host's pools can reach — toolchains, vault tool directories and plugin archives — on the host before a dispatch needs them (ADR-164 D9). Unset means it does; false turns it off for a host whose disk cannot afford it. The daemon places when the runner's own applied report says it is on: on each reload or vault mount that changes a pool's reach, on each connection, and after a rollout confirms the host's new build, in parallel across hosts within runner_link { rollout { max_transfers } }. Toolchains and plugin archives go as tera toolchain sync --host provisions them, and vault tool directories by a frame naming their digests, which the host pulls as a dispatch would. Off, the host is sent neither, and refuses a frame that reaches it anyway. A plaintext link, which takes no host policy, is pre-placed on by nothing. A host still pre-placing stays eligible for work, and a dispatch that needs what is under way joins that transfer. |
| `cache_cap` | string | no | — | — | — | Bounds what the host keeps of vault tool directories and relayed plugin archives (ADR-164 D10): over the bound it evicts least recently used first, and never a digest a dispatch record names or one pre-placed for a pool the host is in. Toolchain stores keep their own retention. Same size grammar as git_mirror_store_cap, positive; unset keeps everything, and "0" is refused rather than read as unbounded. Applied live: the runner checks it after each pull, each dispatch and each prefetch, and on a tick. A dispatch record is every digest an in-flight dispatch or provisioning plan on the host names. Until the host has received its pre-placement pins from a prefetch, it cannot show an entry unpinned and evicts nothing, unless its applied preplace is off. Relayed archives are bounded as the entries kept in a toolchain store's archive cache; the store's installed content is never evicted. |
